tagline.text: A roughly 140-foot "mother of all falls" deep in the forest of San Luis, Aurora

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300–700 (entrance, guide and tricycle, per person from Baler)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL), about 5–7 hours by road

children.text: Ditumabo Falls is a large waterfall of about 140 feet hidden in the forest of San Luis, Aurora, known locally as "Mother Falls." You ride a tricycle from Baler and then walk 20–30 minutes across streams to reach a wide pool of cold water.

Ditumabo Falls lies in Barangay Ditumabo in San Luis, Aurora. It is usually bundled into Baler itineraries, but administratively it belongs to the neighboring town of San Luis, not Baler. Locals call it "Mother Falls," and travel accounts give its height as about 140 feet (about
). Below the falls is a wide, cold pool that looks dammed, and some visitors swim in it.
Getting there is half the trip. From the parking area or the end of the road, you walk in for about
20–30 minutes

. Accounts differ in wording, but they agree on a flat or gently sloping forest trail plus river crossings over boulders. Beside the trail run thick metal pipes that carry water from the falls to a small hydroelectric plant, and a concrete-paved section means the falls are close. It is near Baler town, so it suits travelers who came to surf and want to spend one afternoon on a side trip.

A few things to keep in mind when reading about it. Some accounts come from visits in 2004 and 2015, so the trail conditions and fees may differ from today. For example, an older account says you must walk about 2 km after the first stream crossing, while recent accounts say it is about 20–30 minutes from the entrance. The access may have been improved to shorten the walk, but this is unconfirmed, so ask your guide or the caretaker about the current route.

This is not a developed resort but a natural attraction managed by local residents. There are simple eateries and stalls and some parking near the entrance, but you should assume there are no changing rooms or lifeguards at the falls. In exchange it is uncrowded, with dense forest and the sound of the falls, a contrast to Baler's seaside scenery. One last piece of planning advice: the visit takes only three to four hours including transport, so plan it as a half day and fit other Baler sights into the rest of your time. If you have energy to spare, see the falls first thing in the morning and take a surf lesson in the afternoon. A surfboard rental with an instructor is quoted at about
per hour.

A column of water about 140 feet high drops between cliffs into a wide pool. It is the kind of scale that makes you understand why locals call it Mother Falls. Right after the rainy season the flow is stronger, and in the dry season it can thin out.
The pool below the falls is very cold. One reviewer wrote that the water was too cold to get in. If you plan to swim, bring dry clothes and a towel so you do not get chilled.
The trek crosses several rocky streams and passes small waterfalls and brooks. There are wooden footways in places, so the walk is not hard, but expect your feet to get wet.
Thick metal pipes that carry the falls' water to a small hydroelectric plant run along the trail. They are an unusual sight in the mountains and also serve as a sign that you are getting close.
Local residents act as guides at the entrance. A guide shows you the safe route and may take your photos. Guide fees vary from ₱200 to 300 depending on the account, so confirm on site.

blocks.title: An afternoon to pair with surfing

children.text: Because it is close to Baler town, many travelers surf or visit Diguisit Beach in the morning and see the falls in the afternoon. Check the entrance closing time so you arrive in time.

Caunayan Falls in San Luis is only about a 5-minute walk from the parking area, so it is much easier to reach and the water is shallow. It is an alternative if you are short on time or traveling with children. Note that the current is reportedly strong in places.
Eat breakfast in Baler town, then hire a tricycle or van to Barangay Ditumabo. The ride is about
20–45 minutes
depending on the account, so allow some extra time.
Pay the entrance fee and parking at the entrance and find a guide. Change into sandals or trekking shoes that can get wet.
Start walking with your guide. For about
20–30 minutes
you pass forest trail and stream crossings. When you reach concrete-paved path, the falls are near.
Take photos and rest in front of the falls. If you go into the water, watch out for slippery rocks.
Walk back, have a snack at the stall near the entrance, and return to Baler.
Have lunch at a restaurant in Baler town, then spend the afternoon at Sabang Beach or sightseeing in town.
One account says the falls are open from about 8 AM to 4 PM. After rain the streams can rise and become dangerous, so follow your guide's judgment.
Head from Baler toward San Luis and visit Caunayan Falls first (via Amatorio Resort). It is about a 5-minute walk from the entrance.
Move on to Barangay Ditumabo, register at the entrance and start the trek.
After seeing the falls, have lunch at the stall near the entrance.
Return to Baler to rest at your lodging or surf.
Fees and opening hours for both falls differ between accounts, so check with your lodging or a guide before you go.

for about

By car the distance from Manila is about
. The route via the Maharlika Highway is about
230 km
, and the route using the Central Luzon Link Expressway (CLLEX) is about
268 km
. Accounts say it takes 5–6 hours.
You can also take a Cabanatuan-bound bus and transfer to a Baler-bound bus.
If you leave Manila in the morning and arrive around noon, you can still use the first afternoon.

items.title: From Baler to the falls entrance

children.text: From Baler town to Barangay Ditumabo is about
20–45 minutes
by tricycle or van. Accounts quote about
round trip by tricycle.
If you come from the Cabanatuan side, the jump-off is a dirt road on the right just after the San Luis bridge. Tell the bus driver to drop you at Ditumabo.
Vehicles cannot go all the way to the falls. The tricycle driver drops you where the road turns rough, and you walk from there.

Climate averages for the Baler area show that September–December are the wettest months and August and February are relatively drier. The falls have the most water after the rainy season, but stream crossings can become dangerous. Right after heavy rain, talk to your guide and change your plans if needed.

A good time to go is the dry season, when clear days follow one another. If you visit Baler during the surf season of October–April, it works well to surf in the morning and visit the falls in the afternoon. The trail is said to get slippery in the afternoon from wet visitors, so go in the morning if you can.
Baler's average daytime high is about
and the nightly low about

, with high humidity of around 85%. It is a wet region with about 3,357 mm of rain a year, so the forest floor is often damp even on clear days. The falls' water is always cold, but at midday heat the temperature feels welcome.

There is almost no lodging near the falls, and most places to stay cluster around Sabang Beach in Baler. Accounts often mention Costa Pacifica, Playa Azul, Blue Coco Baler Beach House and Nalu Surf Camp. Baler fills up quickly on weekends, holidays and in summer, so book ahead.

Stalls at the entrance sell simple snacks, and you eat proper meals in Baler town. Bayler View is a restaurant overlooking Sabang Beach, and Kubli Bistro is known as a restaurant in the Poblacion. Suman de Baler, a local treat of purple yam and glutinous rice, is also worth trying. Opening hours can change, so check.

Baler is a small town, and some accounts say a sustainable tourism development fee (SEDF) of ₱100 per person is charged, but this is unconfirmed, so ask the tourism office or your lodging after you arrive. Book meals and lodging before weekends and long holidays. One guide advises finishing your tour early to catch the 2 PM Genesis bus back to Manila, so check the last bus times at the terminal.
Sandals or trekking shoes that can get wet are a must. Flip-flops are risky on slippery rocks.
Bring water, snacks, a waterproof bag, a change of clothes and a towel. There are few proper changing facilities on site.
Bring insect repellent and sunscreen. Mosquitoes can be a problem on forest trails.
Going in the morning means the trail is less slippery and less crowded.
A guide is close to a necessity. They show you the way and tell you the condition of the streams.
Carry cash in small bills. Entrance, guide and snack payments are mostly cash.
Carry your trash out and do not touch facilities along the trail.
ATMs are scarce in Baler, so withdraw cash in Manila or right after you arrive.
The trail has stream crossings and wet rocks. It is especially slippery on rainy days or in the afternoon, so follow your guide's judgment and turn back if the water has risen.
The water below the falls is very cold. Staying in long can lower your body temperature.
Near the hydroelectric facilities, follow the caretaker's instructions and do not go close to the equipment.
Fees, hours and walking distances differ between accounts and may not be accurate, so check with your lodging or a guide before visiting.
The Baler area is in the typhoon belt. Change your plans if there is a weather warning.
When swimming, check the depth and current first and do not go into deep water alone.
The birthplace of Philippine surfing and the center of Aurora, with lodging and restaurants. It is about
20–45 minutes
by tricycle from town to the falls entrance.
Located in Barangay L. Pimentel, San Luis, it is easy to reach, about 5 minutes from the parking area. The water is shallow and cold.
A waterfall at the end of a short climb and a rocky shoreline in Zabali, Baler, easy to combine on the same day.
A balete tree about 600 years old in the neighboring town of Maria Aurora. It is about
30 minutes
by car from Baler.
